experiments.name: build-time
experiments.title: Profile build time
experiments.question: How fast is a windowed Z-curve profile built, from 20 kbp to 10.24 Mbp?
experiments.note: Debug build. The manuscript quoted 39.6–49.7 M bases/s from an earlier run of this benchmark; the committed table (2026-09-11) gives 23.2–40.9. A4 reruns it in Release.

explain.asks: How long does it take to turn a DNA sequence into its Z-curve profile? A profile is built once per genome and then stored, so this sets what profiling a catalogue costs.
explain.how: Random DNA, generated from a fixed seed so the run can be repeated, at 8 lengths from 20 kbp to 10.24 Mbp. Each length is profiled 5 times on a 4-core laptop processor (i7-10510U).
verdict: A measurement: no rule. Building runs at 23 to 41 million bases per second: 0.16 s for a 5 Mbp bacterial-size genome, 0.27 s at 10.24 Mbp. The time grows in step with length.

Timed in a Debug build on a laptop processor; the released software runs faster. The manuscript quoted an earlier Debug run of the same benchmark; this page shows the run whose table is published here.
explain.meaning: Profiling is a single pass over the sequence, so its cost grows in step with length and stays small: a whole bacterial genome takes a fraction of a second.
methodNote: Alignment has nothing to build but pays again at every comparison. The profile moves the work into one pass per genome; every later comparison uses only the stored profile.
The table also times CAT, the earlier method, which built about 6.6 times slower in this run.

explain.asks: Once two genomes are profiled, how long does comparing them take? A search compares a query with many stored genomes, so this sets how fast a search can be.
explain.how: Pairs of random DNA profiles from 20 kbp to 10.24 Mbp (40 to 20,480 windows of 500 bases), lined up from their starts and compared 5 times each, on the same laptop processor.

experiments.name: reliability-at-scale
experiments.title: Score against known mutation rate
experiments.question: Does the score fall steadily with the substitution rate, at every length?
experiments.note: Substitutions only; indels are planned (A10). 5 seeds per length.

explain.asks: Does the score drop steadily as two sequences differ more, and does that hold at every length? A score is only useful for ranking if more differences always mean a lower score.
explain.how: Random DNA at 8 lengths, 20 kbp to 10.24 Mbp. Each is compared with copies in which a known share of bases (1% to 50%) has been substituted, and with an unrelated random sequence; 5 seeds per length. Only substitutions: insertions and deletions aren't tested here.
verdict: A measurement: no rule. At every length the score falls in the same order: 0.990 at 1% substituted, 0.983 at 3%, 0.978 at 5%, 0.968 at 10%, 0.955 at 20%, 0.945 at 30% and 0.929 at 50%, against about 0.90 for an unrelated sequence.
The spread between seeds is tiny at genome lengths (under 0.0003 at 10.24 Mbp) and larger for short sequences (up to 0.010 at 20 kbp).
meaning: The score ranks reliably: more differences always mean a lower score, and the same difference gives the same score whatever the length.
Its range is narrow, though: unrelated random sequences still score about 0.90, because they have the same overall composition. Read the score by its rank, not as a percentage identity.
explain.methodNote: An alignment's identity falls much further for unrelated DNA (to about 0.56 with this project's alignment measure). That is why the platform ranks hits and gives each a p and E value from a null distribution, instead of showing the raw score as a similarity.

charts.title: Score against the share of bases substituted, at three lengths
charts.help: The mean of 5 seeds at each rate. The dashed line is the score against an unrelated random sequence.
charts.read: The three lengths lie on top of each other: the score depends on how much changed, not on how long the sequence is. All other lengths are in the table.

terms: Z-curve score

How alike two profiles are, from 0 to 1, at their best-matching offset. Identical sequences score 1; unrelated sequences of similar composition still score high (about 0.9), so the score is read by its rank, not as a percentage.
Substitution
One base replaced by another at the same place, the simplest kind of mutation. Insertions and deletions, which shift everything after them, are a different kind.

experiments.name: nw-accuracy
experiments.title: Accuracy against Needleman–Wunsch
experiments.question: How does the score track global alignment identity from 500 bp to 20 kbp?

explain.asks: How does the Z-curve score compare with the classic measure of similarity, a global alignment (Needleman–Wunsch)? Does it rank pairs the same way as alignment identity?
how: Random DNA from 500 bp to 20 kbp, compared with copies carrying 1% to 50% substitutions and with unrelated random DNA, scored both by the Z-curve profile and by a full global alignment.

Alignment is slow (8.4 s per pair at 20 kbp here), so 10 and 20 kbp were spot-checked with one seed and the shorter lengths run with 5. The alignment measure is matching bases over the shorter length.
verdict: A measurement: no rule. From 5 kbp up, both scores fall in the same order as the substitution rate, so they rank pairs alike. Their scales differ: with half the bases changed, alignment identity is about 0.65 and the Z-curve score about 0.93; for unrelated DNA, 0.56 against 0.90.
At 2 kbp and below the Z-curve score is noisy, with few windows to average, and neighbouring rates can swap places (2 kbp: 20% substituted scores 0.949, 30% scores 0.953).
explain.meaning: For ranking, the profile agrees with alignment wherever the sequences have enough windows; for short sequences it gets noisy. It isn't an identity measure: a score of 0.95 doesn't mean 95% identical.
explain.methodNote: The point of the profile is alignment's ranking without alignment's cost: a 20 kbp pair took 8.4 s to align here and a fraction of a millisecond to compare by profile. The price is resolution: below a few kbp, and between close mutation rates, the profile loses distinctions alignment keeps.

charts.help: The mean of 5 seeds at each substitution rate, scored by the Z-curve profile and by global alignment.
charts.read: Both fall steadily, so they put pairs in the same order; the Z-curve score just uses a much narrower range. Other lengths are in the table.

experiments.name: genome-scale
experiments.title: A 3.1 Gbp genome, streamed
experiments.question: Can a human-sized genome be profiled, searched and stored without loading it as a string?
experiments.note: The compare and reliability rows predate the SIMD rewrite (upper bounds). The manuscript quoted 141.7 ms for the planted fragment; the committed table gives 141.4 ms.

keyNumbers.label: ms to find a planted fragment

explain.asks: A human genome, about 3.1 billion bases, is too large to hold as one piece of text in this software (its limit is about 1.07 billion characters). Can it still be profiled, searched and stored by reading it as a stream?
how: A synthetic 3.1 Gbp sequence, read from a file as a stream and profiled at 500 bp windows: 6.2 million windows. A 2 kbp gene was planted at a known place and then searched for.
Also measured: the profile's size, one whole-against-whole comparison, and the score against copies with 1% to 50% of bases substituted.
verdict: A measurement: no rule. The profile was built in 104 s, 30 million bases per second, most of it spent reading the file (72 s). The planted gene was found at exactly its window, with a score of 1, in 141 ms.

The profile takes 74.4 MB: 83 times less than the sequence as this software holds text (2 bytes per base), about 42 times less than a plain FASTA file (1 byte per base), and about 10 times less than the tightest packing of DNA (2 bits per base).

The score falls steadily with the substitution rate, as at shorter lengths: 0.990 at 1%, 0.929 at 50%, 0.899 for unrelated sequence. The comparison times in the table predate a later speed-up and are upper bounds. Debug build, laptop processor.
explain.meaning: Size is no barrier for the profile: a human-sized genome is profiled in under 2 minutes on a laptop and searched in a fraction of a second, without ever holding the DNA in memory. The platform ingests genomes the same way, which is why it never needs to keep DNA.
explain.methodNote: Streaming works because the method keeps only window summaries, 12 bytes per 500 bases, and while reading only the running sums of the current window. Tools that need the whole sequence, or an index of it, in memory have to hold billions of bases.

experiments.name: distance-matrix
experiments.title: 30 bacteria, all pairs
experiments.question: Do scores order pairs by relationship: same species, genus, phylum, different phylum?

explain.asks: On real genomes, do the scores order pairs by how closely related they are: same species above same genus, above same phylum, above different phyla?
explain.how: The 30 bacterial genomes bundled with the project, all 435 pairs, grouped by relationship from NCBI taxonomy: 1 pair of the same species, 7 of the same genus, 97 of the same phylum and 330 from different phyla. Every pair is compared by its 500 bp profiles.
verdict: A measurement: no rule. The mean scores fall in the expected order: 0.819 same species, 0.791 same genus, 0.757 same phylum, 0.606 different phyla.
The groups overlap a lot: same-phylum pairs range from 0.42 to 0.85, and different-phylum pairs from 0.12 to 0.85. The top two means rest on 1 and 7 pairs.
explain.meaning: On average the score tracks relatedness, but one score alone doesn't tell you the relationship: some pairs from different phyla score as high as close relatives. Much of that overlap is GC content, which makes genomes look alike whatever their ancestry (see 'GC alone as a baseline').
explain.methodNote: Real genomes spread far more widely than random sequences, which all score about 0.90 against each other: differences in composition pull the score down. On real data the score therefore covers a wide range (0.12 to 0.85), though much of it through composition.

experiments.name: external-baseline
experiments.title: Against Mash and FastANI
experiments.question: How do the scores relate to Mash and FastANI on the same 435 pairs?
experiments.note: Mash saturates for distant pairs while the Z-curve stays graded; FastANI returns nothing for most pairs. Mash and FastANI outputs are in results/raw/.

keyNumbers.label: Pearson r with Mash, 22 pairs above its floor

explain.asks: How do our scores relate to two standard tools for comparing genomes, Mash and FastANI, on the same pairs?
how: The 30 bacterial genomes bundled with the project, all 435 pairs, grouped by relationship from NCBI taxonomy: 1 pair of the same species, 7 of the same genus, 97 of the same phylum and 330 from different phyla.

Each pair is scored by our profile, by Mash (as a similarity, 1 minus Mash distance) and by FastANI (average nucleotide identity). Mash and FastANI were run outside the project; their outputs are kept with the results.
verdict: A measurement: no rule. The three behave differently. Mash falls to almost nothing for pairs from different phyla (mean 0.004): beyond a certain distance it gives no signal. FastANI reports only 14 of the 435 pairs, the close ones. Our score stays graded at every distance, from 0.82 for the same species to 0.61 for different phyla.

Where Mash still gives a signal (22 pairs off its floor), the two agree only loosely (Pearson r = 0.39). In this run all 435 pairs took 23 s with our 500 bp profiles, 6 s with Mash and 93 s with FastANI, the last two in Docker, so not timed on equal terms.
explain.meaning: Mash and FastANI are built for close relatives and are very good there, but say little about distant pairs. The Z-curve score keeps giving a graded answer at any distance, though a weaker one: for finding close relatives Mash ranks better ('Retrieval against Mash').
explain.methodNote: This is the profile's niche: it never saturates, so it can still order pairs from different phyla, where Mash says 0 and FastANI says nothing. Whether that graded signal is ancestry or mostly GC content is what 'GC alone as a baseline' and 'Beyond GC, on same-GC pairs' test.

experiments.name: retrieval-classification
experiments.title: Retrieval against Mash
experiments.question: Ranking pairs by score, how well are same-genus and same-phylum pairs found, against Mash?
experiments.note: Mash ranks better.

explain.asks: If all pairs are ranked by score, how well do related pairs come first? And how does that compare with Mash?
explain.how: The 30 bacterial genomes bundled with the project, all 435 pairs, grouped by relationship from NCBI taxonomy: 1 pair of the same species, 7 of the same genus, 97 of the same phylum and 330 from different phyla. Two questions: same genus or closer against the rest, and same phylum against different phyla. Each is scored as AUC, and at the best cut-off as precision, recall and F1.
verdict: A measurement: no rule. Mash ranks better: AUC 0.969 against our 0.835 for same genus, and 0.802 against 0.789 for same phylum. At the best cut-off, Mash's F1 is 0.48 against 0.23 for same genus, and 0.75 against 0.56 for same phylum.
Only 8 pairs share a genus, so the genus numbers are uncertain.
explain.meaning: For telling close relatives from the rest, Mash, which compares the short words genomes actually share, is clearly better than the profile. The profile's case rests elsewhere: speed and size, no DNA kept, graded scores at any distance, and placing fragments, which Mash doesn't do.
explain.methodNote: A clear result against the method as a stand-alone relative-finder: on close relatives, word-based Mash ranks better. It is reported as such in the manuscript.

charts.title: Ranking related pairs first (AUC): Z-curve and Mash
charts.help: How well each method ranks related pairs above the rest. Bars start at 0.5, a coin toss.
charts.read: Mash is well ahead for the same genus and slightly ahead for the same phylum. Precision, recall and F1 at the best cut-off are in the second table.

terms: AUC

A score for how well a ranking puts the right items first: 0.5 is a coin toss, 1 is perfect. Here it is the chance that a randomly picked related pair scores closer than a randomly picked unrelated pair.
Mash
A widely used tool that compares genomes by the share of short words (k-mers) they have in common, estimated from a small random sample of them (MinHash).
F1
One number combining precision (how many pairs called related really are) and recall (how many related pairs were found); 1 is perfect.

experiments.name: window-size
experiments.title: Window size sensitivity
experiments.question: How do 250, 500, 1,000 and 2,000 bp windows change the relationship levels?

explain.asks: The profile uses 500 bp windows. Does that choice matter? How do 250, 1,000 and 2,000 bp windows change the scores at each level of relationship?
explain.how: The 30 bacterial genomes bundled with the project, all 435 pairs, grouped by relationship from NCBI taxonomy: 1 pair of the same species, 7 of the same genus, 97 of the same phylum and 330 from different phyla. The genomes are profiled at four window sizes, and the mean score per level is compared.
verdict: A measurement: no rule. Larger windows raise every score (same species 0.785 at 250 bp to 0.870 at 2,000 bp; different phyla 0.587 to 0.631) but keep the same order between levels.
The gap between same genus and different phyla widens a little with window size: 0.172 at 250 bp, 0.185 at 500 bp, 0.206 at 2,000 bp.
explain.meaning: The window size shifts the scale but not the order, so 500 bp isn't a fragile choice. What matters more is how many windows the shorter genome has ('Window count decides quality').
explain.methodNote: Larger windows average away more noise, so all scores rise towards 1; smaller windows keep finer detail but more noise. The ladder's coarser levels (2, 8, 32 kbp) are derived from the 500 bp profile.

experiments.name: single-point-ceiling
experiments.title: The single-point ceiling (CAT)
experiments.question: Does a single-point profile tell phiX174 from lambda phage?
experiments.note: CAT was removed from the code; it is at commit e152aa4.
experiments.command: git checkout e152aa4, then the phage motivating example in SequenceAnaliseTests

explain.asks: Before the Z-curve profile, this project used CAT, which reduced a whole sequence to a single point of three numbers. Can a single point tell two clearly unrelated genomes apart?
explain.how: Two well-known phages that share no ancestry, phiX174 (5,386 bp) and lambda (48,502 bp), compared by their CAT profiles.
explain.verdict: A measurement: no rule. CAT scored them 0.998, as if nearly identical.
explain.meaning: A single point summarising a whole sequence becomes, as the sequence grows, a measure of base composition alone, so unrelated sequences of similar composition become indistinguishable. Small changes to the single point didn't fix it; keeping a summary for every window along the sequence did. That is why CAT was replaced by the windowed Z-curve profile.
explain.methodNote: The example that motivated the current method: the failure that windowing solves ('Fixed window size, not fixed count'). CAT is no longer in the code; it is kept in the project's history.

experiments.name: windowing-strategy
experiments.title: Fixed window size, not fixed count
experiments.question: Does a fixed window size keep unrelated pairs from drifting together as sequences grow?

explain.asks: Any profile built from composition risks CAT's failure: as sequences grow, random fluctuations average out and unrelated sequences drift together. Does fixing the window size, rather than the number of windows, stop that drift?
how: Pairs of unrelated random sequences, compared at a short and a much longer length by three constructions: a single endpoint (the whole sequence's composition), a fixed number of 20 checkpoints along the sequence, and fixed windows of 500 bp. A score that rises with length for unrelated pairs is drift.
A second test: a sequence with an AT-rich first half and a GC-rich second half, against the same bases shuffled. The composition is identical; only the order differs.
verdict: Pass. No numeric rule was written down; the claim was that fixed windows keep the unrelated score from rising with length. It doesn't rise: 0.896 at 2 kbp, 0.897 at 200 kbp. With 20 fixed checkpoints it drifts from 0.911 to 0.988 over the same range, and the single endpoint scores 0.972 already at 5 kbp and 0.983 at 50 kbp.
On the shuffled sequence, the endpoint scores 1, seeing no difference at all, while following the path at 20 checkpoints scores 0.66.
explain.meaning: A window of fixed size always averages the same number of bases, so its noise stays the same however long the genome; more windows just add evidence. With a fixed count, each window grows with the genome, its noise shrinks, and every sequence starts to look like its average composition.
explain.methodNote: This is the design choice at the heart of the method, and what separates it from single-number composition summaries such as GC or the earlier CAT: the number of windows grows with the genome, so the profile keeps local information at any length.

A way of writing DNA as a path in three dimensions, one axis for each pair of base properties: purine (A, G) against pyrimidine (C, T), amino (A, C) against keto (G, T), and strong (G, C) against weak (A, T) pairing. The third axis is GC content.

experiments.name: window-count
experiments.title: Window count decides quality
experiments.question: How few windows can the shorter genome keep before retrieval suffers?
experiments.note: Bacteria lose no AUC down to a median of about 4 windows; with 0 windows Compare returns 0.

explain.asks: The ladder compares genomes at coarser windows to save time. How few windows can the shorter genome have before the results suffer?
explain.how: The 30 bundled bacteria (435 pairs) and 31 bundled viruses (465 pairs), profiled at windows from 500 bp up to 2 Mbp, each level derived from the 500 bp profile by merging windows. At each size: AUC for close relatives (same genus) and for related ones (same phylum for bacteria, same family for viruses), and how many windows the shorter genome keeps.
verdict: A measurement: no rule. Bacteria keep their AUC down to a median of about 4 windows in the shorter genome (same genus 0.835 at 500 bp, 0.851 at 512 kbp). Viruses fall gently: same genus 0.881 with a median of 18 windows, 0.850 with 2.

When the shorter genome has no complete window the comparison returns 0, and the pair looks unrelated: with 1 Mbp windows that happens to 84 bacterial pairs. Virus families are weak at every size (AUC about 0.60).
explain.meaning: What decides quality is the number of windows, not their size: a comparison needs only a handful. That lets long genomes be compared at coarse levels, hundreds of times faster, with no loss ('The multi-resolution ladder'). Same-family viruses are hard for this method at any resolution.
explain.methodNote: This sets the ladder's rule: compare at the coarsest level that still leaves the shorter genome 8 windows, a margin above the 4 or so where bacteria start to lose.

experiments.title: The multi-resolution ladder
experiments.question: Comparing at the coarsest level that keeps 8 windows: same accuracy, less time?
experiments.note: All pairs in 8.6 ms instead of 23.5 s.

explain.asks: Comparing at the finest level (500 bp) is accurate but slow for long genomes. If each pair is compared at the coarsest level that still leaves the shorter genome 8 windows, is accuracy kept, and how much time is saved?
explain.how: The 30 bundled bacteria and 31 bundled viruses, all pairs, compared once at 500 bp and once by the ladder rule over its 500 bp, 2, 8 and 32 kbp levels.
verdict: Pass. No numeric rule was written down; the aim was the same accuracy in less time. Bacteria keep their accuracy (same genus AUC 0.853 against 0.835 at 500 bp; same phylum 0.783 against 0.789), and all 435 pairs, compared at 32 kbp, take 8.6 ms instead of 23.5 s, about 2,700 times faster.
Viruses, mostly too short for the coarse levels, gain a little (same genus 0.895 against 0.881) in half the time.
explain.meaning: Coarse windows lose almost nothing for whole-genome comparison, so the catalogue search compares at the coarsest level a query allows. Scores from different levels aren't on the same scale, so a search ranks every candidate at one level, chosen by the query.
explain.methodNote: Multiple resolutions come almost for free with window averages: a coarse window is just the average of its neighbouring fine ones, so the whole ladder is computed from the 500 bp profile without going back to the DNA.

experiments.name: gc-baseline
experiments.title: GC alone as a baseline
experiments.question: How close does GC content alone get to the Z-curve's retrieval?
experiments.note: The genus AUC rests on 8 positive pairs (CI about ±0.17).

explain.asks: GC content alone is the simplest way to compare genomes. How close does it get to the Z-curve score at finding relatives?
explain.how: The 30 bacterial genomes bundled with the project, all 435 pairs, grouped by relationship from NCBI taxonomy: 1 pair of the same species, 7 of the same genus, 97 of the same phylum and 330 from different phyla. The pairs are ranked by the Z-curve score and by the plain difference in GC, with AUC for same genus against the rest and for same phylum against other phyla.
verdict: A measurement: no rule. GC alone does about as well: 0.852 against the Z-curve's 0.835 for same genus, 0.769 against 0.789 for same phylum.
With only 8 same-genus pairs, the genus difference is well within chance (about ±0.17).
explain.meaning: On these genomes, most of what the score sees is GC. That raises the question the next test answers: does the score add anything once GC is equal? ('Beyond GC, on same-GC pairs': yes, at family and phylum level.)
explain.methodNote: A plain baseline the method has to beat, and on all pairs it barely does. The profile's advantage shows only on pairs GC can't separate.

experiments.name: gc-stratum
experiments.title: Beyond GC, on same-GC pairs
experiments.question: On pairs of nearly equal GC, does the score still separate taxa?
experiments.note: 437 catalogue genomes. All pairs: Spearman 0.993 between 1 − Compare and |ΔGC|. Same-GC pairs: ties GC at genus, beats it at family (+0.074) and phylum (+0.10 to +0.14).

explain.asks: Two genomes with similar GC content tend to look alike to any score built from composition. So is our score just measuring GC? This test asks whether it still tells related genomes from unrelated ones where GC can't help: among pairs whose GC is nearly the same.
how: 437 bacterial and archaeal genomes from the catalogue, every pair compared: 95,266 pairs. Each pair is labelled related or not at three levels: same genus, same family, same phylum. Two scores rank the pairs: our Z-curve score (at its 32 kbp level) and the plain difference in GC. How well each ranks related pairs above unrelated ones is measured as AUC.
The pairs are then split by how far apart their GC is. The key group is pairs within 2 GC points of each other, where GC by itself has almost nothing to go on.
verdict: A measurement: no rule was set in advance. It shows two things.
Over all pairs, the score follows GC very closely (rank correlation 0.993 between our distance and the GC difference), and GC alone ranks same-genus pairs slightly better (AUC 0.905 against 0.895).

On pairs of nearly equal GC, where GC is close to guessing, the Z-curve score still finds families (AUC 0.635 against 0.562; difference +0.074, interval +0.008 to +0.129) and phyla (0.610 against 0.506; +0.104, interval +0.054 to +0.152). Within a genus the two tie (0.614 against 0.610).
explain.meaning: Between genomes of different GC, most of what the score sees is GC, which is why it agrees with GC over all pairs. Where GC is the same, the score still carries ancestry at family and phylum level, so it holds information GC doesn't. On same-GC pairs within a genus neither score does well (both about 0.61).
methodNote: Methods that reduce a genome to one composition number, such as GC, can't tell apart two genomes with the same value. Our profile keeps all three Z-curve axes for every window along the genome, not just GC. This test is the direct check that this adds something: on pairs GC can't separate, the profile still finds families and phyla.

It also marks the limit plainly: over all pairs GC alone does about as well, so the profile's advantage is on the hard pairs, not on average. Whether the gain comes from the two non-GC axes or from their order along the genome, this test doesn't separate.

experiments.name: strand-rotation
experiments.title: Strand and rotation
experiments.question: Does a genome against its own reverse complement or rotation still look identical?
experiments.note: It scores like a different strain: the query is compared on both strands since.

keyNumbers.label: K-12 vs itself rotated by half

explain.asks: A circular bacterial chromosome can be deposited from either strand and from any starting point. Does the score see E. coli K-12 against its own reverse complement, or against itself started halfway round, as the same genome?
explain.how: E. coli K-12 compared with its reverse complement, with itself rotated by half its length, and with both together; for scale, against another E. coli strain (O157:H7) and another genus (Bacillus subtilis). Scored at 500 bp and at the 32 kbp level.
verdict: A measurement: no rule. It doesn't see them as the same: against its reverse complement K-12 scores 0.815, against itself rotated by half 0.814, both together 0.819. That is the same as against a different strain (O157:H7, 0.819) and not far above a different genus (B. subtilis, 0.762).
At the 32 kbp level the picture is the same: 0.93 to 0.94, against 0.95 for O157:H7.
explain.meaning: The profile reads a genome in one direction from one starting point, so the same chromosome deposited differently looks like a different strain. The platform therefore compares every query on both strands, and lays out circular chromosomes from their replication origin ('Replication origin from the profile').
explain.methodNote: A limit of any profile that follows the sequence in order, which composition-only methods (GC, or Mash's strand-independent word counts) don't have. It is handled around the profile, by searching both strands and fixing the starting point.

charts.title: E. coli K-12 against variants of itself and other genomes
charts.help: The Z-curve score at 500 bp and at the 32 kbp level, K-12 forward against each variant.
charts.read: K-12 against its own reverse complement or rotation scores no higher than against O157:H7, a different strain.

terms: Z-curve score

How alike two profiles are, from 0 to 1, at their best-matching offset. Identical sequences score 1; unrelated sequences of similar composition still score high (about 0.9), so the score is read by its rank, not as a percentage.
Reverse complement
The same DNA read from the other strand: reversed, with A and T, and C and G, swapped. A genome can be deposited either way round.

experiments.name: origin-rotation
experiments.title: Replication origin from the profile
experiments.question: Does the minimum of the cumulative GC skew find the origin, and does rotating there restore identity?

keyNumbers.label: K-12 vs itself rotated, as stored (32 kbp)

explain.asks: Can the profile itself tell where a bacterial chromosome's replication origin is, so that every circular chromosome can be laid out from the same starting point?
how: Two of the profile's axes give the GC skew directly (x minus y), so its running sum along the chromosome has its lowest point near the origin. E. coli K-12 is compared with copies of itself started elsewhere and on the other strand, before and after both are rotated to start at that point.
The 30 bundled bacteria are then checked: rotating every genome shouldn't harm comparisons between different genomes.
verdict: Pass. No numeric rule was written down. The lowest point of the running skew lands on K-12's known origin (oriC). After rotating there, K-12 against itself started halfway round scores 0.998 at 32 kbp, up from 0.932, and 0.913 at 500 bp, up from 0.814 (at 500 bp the rotation can't line windows up exactly).
Comparisons between different genomes are unchanged: same-genus AUC 0.831 against 0.835 at 500 bp.
explain.meaning: The profile holds enough of a chromosome's structure to find its own origin, so circular chromosomes can be compared from a common start. The platform stores origin-rotated levels for circular chromosomes of 500 kbp and up; its search scores both layouts and keeps the better.
explain.methodNote: Something composition-only summaries can't offer: because the profile keeps the order of windows, it shows the skew pattern that marks the origin. Here it repairs the profile's own weakness ('Strand and rotation').

charts.title: K-12 against itself: as deposited, and rotated to the origin
charts.help: The Z-curve score at the 32 kbp level, before and after both genomes are rotated to start at the found origin.

Variant: K-12 rotated by a multiple of 500 bp

experiments.name: genome-moments
experiments.title: Moments on genome windows
experiments.question: Do Legendre moments help on the unanchored genome ladder, as they do on genes?
experiments.note: Retrieval unchanged (0.830 / 0.794); arbitrary-phase localization drops. The genome ladder keeps means.

explain.asks: Each window of our genome profile is summarised by the average of its three Z-curve axes. For genes, also describing how the curve bends inside each window (Legendre moments) made protein search better. Does the same help for whole genomes?
how: Two tasks on the 30 bundled bacterial genomes, each run once with window averages (3 numbers per window) and once with moments (9 numbers per window).

Retrieval: rank all 435 genome pairs, and measure as AUC how well same-genus and same-phylum pairs come first. Localization: cut 600 fragments of 4 and 10 kbp, unchanged or with 2% of their bases changed, and check whether each is found at its true place. Fragments are cut either at a window boundary or anywhere, which is what real fragments are like.
verdict: Fail: moments don't do for genomes what they did for genes. No numeric rule was set; the change was to be kept only if it helped.

Retrieval barely moves (same genus 0.830 against 0.835 with averages, same phylum 0.794 against 0.789). Fragments cut anywhere are found 63.7% of the time with moments, against 94.5% with averages, over the four fragment settings.
explain.meaning: Moments describe the shape of the curve inside a window, and that shape depends on where the window starts. Gene windows always start at the start codon, so the same gene gives the same shapes. Genome windows start wherever the sequence starts, so a fragment's windows are shifted against the genome's and their shapes no longer match. Averages hardly change with that shift. So the genome profile keeps averages, and moments are used only for genes.
explain.methodNote: A negative result that shaped the method. It shows that a richer summary of each window isn't automatically better, and it is why the genome profile and the gene profile summarise their windows differently.

experiments.name: catalogue-localization
experiments.title: Localizing fragments over the catalogue
experiments.question: Is a fragment's source found among all records, at the coarsest level leaving 4 windows?
experiments.note: Source in the top 100 in 30/30 at 10–200 kbp, 23–26/30 at 4 kbp. Cached 0.17–1.14 s per fragment.

explain.asks: Given a stretch of DNA from 4 to 200 kbp, can the platform find which stored genome it comes from, searching the whole catalogue from profiles alone?
how: 30 fragments per length and kind, cut at random places from the bundled bacteria and viruses, half of them reverse-complemented. Each was scanned against every stored record at least as long (the local catalogue on 2026-10-22), at the coarsest level leaving the fragment 4 windows, on both strands and at every starting phase; the 100 best were then refined at 500 bp.
The fragment's true source record was known from its DNA's fingerprint (SHA-256). Counted: the source in the top 100, the source first, and a genome of the same genus first.
verdict: Pass. No numeric rule was written down. From 10 kbp the source is in the top 100 for every fragment (30 of 30), for bacteria and viruses alike; at 4 kbp for 23 (bacteria) and 26 (viruses) of 30.

The source itself comes first more often as fragments grow: bacteria 11 of 30 at 4 kbp, 28 to 30 from 32 kbp; viruses 13 at 4 kbp, 18 to 26 from 8 kbp. A genome of the same genus comes first for all 30 from 20 kbp. A search takes 0.17 to 1.0 s (median) with the catalogue's profiles in memory.
explain.meaning: Fragments of 10 kbp and up are reliably traced to their genome, and from 20 kbp to the right genus. When the source isn't first, a genome of the same genus usually is. Short fragments (4 kbp) are the limit.
explain.methodNote: Placing a fragment in a whole catalogue normally means aligning it against every stored sequence, which requires keeping the DNA. Here it runs on stored profiles only, over tens of thousands of records, in under a second.

experiments.name: localization-validation
experiments.title: True start of real fragments
experiments.question: Are 2, 10 and 50 kbp fragments of real genomes placed at their true start, on both strands?
experiments.note: 40/40 at 10 and 50 kbp; 14/20 at 2 kbp inside a named record.

explain.asks: When a real fragment is found, is it placed at its true starting position in the genome, and on the right strand?
explain.how: Fragments of 2, 10 and 50 kbp cut from the bundled bacteria at known positions, 10 per length, each searched on both strands (20 searches per length). 10 and 50 kbp fragments were searched over the whole catalogue; 2 kbp ones, too short for that, inside the named genome only.
verdict: Pass. No numeric rule was written down. At 10 and 50 kbp all 40 searches found the source genome, the right strand and the true start. At 2 kbp, inside the named genome, the right genome and strand were found every time and the true start in 14 of 20; the other 6 were placed elsewhere in the same genome.
explain.meaning: For fragments of 10 kbp and up, a hit means the right place, not just the right genome. At 2 kbp a fragment has only 4 windows, and similar stretches elsewhere in the genome can match as well.
explain.methodNote: The profile places fragments to the window and then to the base by trying every starting phase, so position comes out of the same few numbers used for similarity; no index of the DNA is needed.

experiments.name: somatic-mutations
experiments.title: Somatic point mutations
experiments.question: Can the score see tumour-like point mutations between two copies of a genome?
experiments.note: 100 per Mbp move the score 9–620× less than the closest strain pair.

keyNumbers.label: score change at 100 mutations per Mbp

explain.asks: Could the platform tell a tumour genome from the normal genome of the same person? Tumours carry somatic point mutations: about 1 to 10 per million bases in most, up to about 100 in hypermutated ones.
how: No human DNA is used: E. coli K-12's chromosome stands in for a genome. Substitutions were planted at 1, 10, 100 and 1,000 per Mbp, either uniformly or as C→T changes at CpG sites (the commonest somatic pattern), 5 seeds each.

Each copy is scored against the original as the platform would: the profile at 500 bp, the profile through the ladder, and the dinucleotide signature. Four pairs of real, closely related strains (K-12 against O157:H7, and so on) give the scale.
verdict: Fail. The rule, agreed beforehand: if 100 mutations per Mbp move the score less than the closest strain pair does, tumour genomes aren't worth loading for this method.

At 100 per Mbp the score moves 9 to 620 times less than between the closest strains, depending on the measure: the dinucleotide signature with CpG changes comes closest, the 500 bp profile is least sensitive.
explain.meaning: Point mutations at tumour rates are far below what a composition profile can see: they change a few hundred bases out of millions, while strains differ over whole regions. Finding somatic mutations needs read alignment to a reference, a different kind of tool.
explain.methodNote: A limit stated plainly: the profile summarises regions, so it is blind to scattered single-base changes at these rates.

experiments.name: back-translation
experiments.title: Protein search by back-translation
experiments.question: Can a back-translated protein be localized in genome windows?
experiments.note: No-go: genome windows reach at most 3.3% top-1; per-gene profiles pooled over 30 bacteria at most 42.5%.

explain.asks: Before the gene profile existed: can a protein be found in the genome profiles by translating it back into DNA? A protein's DNA isn't known exactly, since most amino acids have several codons, so the back-translation has to guess.
how: Proteins from the 30 bundled bacteria, back-translated several ways: the commonest codon, codons drawn by the genome's own usage, codons drawn uniformly at random. The real gene DNA gives the upper bound and random DNA the floor.

First route: place the guessed DNA in the genome profile's 500 bp windows. Second: compare it with per-gene profiles (each gene profiled on its own, codon positions 1 and 2) pooled over all 30 bacteria.
verdict: Fail: judged a no-go; no numeric rule was written down. In genome windows the best back-translation put the gene first for at most 3.3% of proteins, though the real gene DNA is found 77% of the time (3 kbp genes).

Against per-gene profiles pooled over 30 bacteria, back-translation that doesn't know the genome's codon usage found the gene first for 42.5% of 1.5 kbp genes and 13.2% of 999 bp ones. Knowing the codon usage, which a real query wouldn't, raised that to 74% and 40%.
explain.meaning: Guessing codons loses too much of the signal. What came next: turn the protein straight into the profile its gene would most likely have, averaged over all its possible codons, and describe each window's shape, not just its average ('The gene profile').
explain.methodNote: A negative result that shaped the gene profile: genome windows, which ignore where genes start, can't carry a protein's signal, and one guessed DNA is too noisy a stand-in for the protein.

charts.help: The share of proteins whose own gene is ranked first, for each way of making a DNA query, at two gene lengths.
charts.read: Only the real DNA is found reliably. Guessed DNA falls far short, and the guesses that do best need the genome's codon usage, which a query protein doesn't come with.

terms: Z-curve gene profile

The per-gene version of the profile: each gene read from its start codon in its coding direction, using codon positions 1 and 2, in windows of 500 bases of gene, each window kept as nine numbers (the moments of its three axes).
Top 1
The right answer is ranked first.

experiments.name: cds-sweep
experiments.title: The gene profile
experiments.question: Which per-gene profile finds a gene from its protein alone?
experiments.note: Adopted: codon positions 1 and 2, windows of 500 bp of gene from the start codon, Legendre moments P0–P2 of x, y, z. Means alone reach 50.2%. Unweighted score; whitened moments reached 93.3% here, and weights were adopted on 2026-11-20 (protein-weights).

explain.asks: What should a gene's profile look like for a gene to be found from its protein alone? This sweep tried which codon positions to use, how long the windows should be, and what to keep for each window.
how: Genes of the bundled bacteria, each profiled from its start codon in its coding direction. The query is the protein's expected profile (no DNA needed), searched among about 16,000 genes of 30 bacteria, with the result extrapolated to catalogue size, and against the matching gene in four related bacteria.
Variants: codon positions, window sizes, and per window either the average of each axis (3 numbers), the average and slope (6), or the average, slope and curvature (9, Legendre moments).
verdict: Pass: adopted. No numeric rule was written down; the best variant was chosen. Codon positions 1 and 2, windows of 500 bases of gene, and three moments per axis (9 numbers) find the right gene first for 91.5% of proteins, against 50.2% with averages alone; extrapolated to catalogue size, 75.7% against 8.1%.
The same query finds the ortholog first in E. coli O157:H7 97.8% of the time, in Shigella 94.8%, Salmonella 88.7% and Klebsiella 87.3%. On 300 random species (225,827 genes), 97.0% top 1.
explain.meaning: Read from the start codon, a gene's profile carries enough of its protein to be found among many thousands of genes and in related species. The shape inside each window, its slope and curvature, is what makes it work: averages alone fail at scale.
methodNote: This is the method's second, newer use: protein search with no alignment and no translated database. At codon position 2, two of the Z-curve axes follow the amino acid's hydropathy (Kyte–Doolittle; r = −0.84 on real gene windows), so a window's average, slope and curvature describe how water-repelling that stretch of protein is and how that changes along it. The gene profile is, in effect, a hydropathy profile read from DNA.
It hasn't been compared with BLASTP or similar tools on the same queries.

experiments.question: Is the right protein family first once the query's own gene, genome, species or genus is removed?

asks: The platform's protein search compares a protein with every stored gene without aligning sequences. The protein is turned into the Z-curve windows its gene would most likely have (averaged over the codons that could encode each amino acid), and these are compared with the genes' stored windows.

An earlier check found the right protein family first for every query, but the query's own gene was in the catalogue and simply found itself. This test removes that shortcut: is the right family still first once the query's own gene, its genome, its species or its genus is taken out?
explain.how: 157 proteins from 6 bacteria, 2 archaea and 2 plasmids, in five length bands from 50 to over 500 amino acids (viruses drop out: their proteins have no family labels). Each is searched four times, each time with more of its relatives removed: its own gene, its whole genome, its species, its genus. A hit counts when the best-scoring gene belongs to the query's protein family. A query counts at a level only if some gene of its family is still left there.
verdict: Pass. The rule, set before the run: if, with the query's species removed, the right family came first for fewer than half the queries in any length band, the claim would shrink to 'finds near-identical genes'. No band fell below half: 77.5% to 91.4%, 84.5% overall.
With the whole genus removed, a harder test the rule didn't judge, the right family is still first for 65.9% and in the top 10 for 79.3%.
explain.meaning: The search finds a protein's family, not just copies of the same gene. With its own species gone, the right family still comes first for about 5 proteins in 6, and with its genus gone, for about 2 in 3. Once the genus is removed it is weakest for short proteins (50–166 aa) and very long ones (over 500 aa), at 55–64%.
methodNote: Protein search usually aligns the protein against translated genes, as BLASTP does. Here nothing is aligned and no DNA is kept: the catalogue holds nine numbers for every 500 bases of each gene, and a protein is compared with those directly. This test shows that this compact form still carries a protein's family across species and genera.
It hasn't been compared head to head with BLASTP on the same queries, so it says nothing about which is more sensitive.

experiments.name: protein-family-tuning
experiments.title: Raising the right family
experiments.question: Do feature weights or a vote over the top hits find the right family more often, with the own genus removed?
experiments.rule: The combination best on the tuning half must gain ≥ 5 points on the test half, 95% genome-bootstrap CI excluding 0, losing ≤ 1 point of exact top-1. Best was 'best hit with a family': +3.1 points (paired CI +1.6 to +5.0; the first run printed −8.7 to +15.3 from an unpaired-bootstrap bug, fixed 2026-11-20). Below +5, so tuning stops.

explain.asks: With the query's own genus removed, the right protein family comes first for about 63% of proteins. Can simple tuning raise that: weighting the 9 window numbers differently, letting the top few hits vote, or taking the best hit that has a family label?
explain.how: 1,143 proteins from 64 genomes of the local catalogue (2026-11-12), split by genome into a tuning half and a test half. Each combination of weighting (equal, averages only, averages and slopes, 1 / variance) and choice (best hit, best hit with a family label, a vote of the top 3, 5 or 10) was tried on the tuning half; the best was judged once on the test half.
verdict: Fail. The rule, set before the run: the best combination on the tuning half must gain at least 5 points on the test half, with its 95% interval (resampling genomes) above zero, and lose at most 1 point of finding the exact gene. The best, 'best hit with a family label', gained 3.1 points (interval +1.6 to +5.0): below 5, so tuning stopped.
Not part of the rule: 1 / variance weights raised finding the exact gene on the test half from 83.7% to 87.8%. That was then tested on its own ('Weighted gene-profile score').
explain.meaning: Re-weighting and voting can't lift family search much further; its limit lies deeper ('Shifted same-family profiles', 'Family label or real homolog'). The weights did help exact-gene search, which was followed up separately.
explain.methodNote: A test built so it couldn't flatter the method: tuned on one half of the genomes and judged once on the other.

explain.meaning: Almost every 'miss' is the same protein found first in another genome, a correct answer for most uses. Where the own gene itself is wanted, it is in the top 10 for 97.6% of queries.

experiments.title: Family label or real homolog
experiments.question: Is the top hit a real homolog, and are the family 'misses' partly label noise?
experiments.rule: If the same-family gene is not detectably homologous in ≥ 10 points more of misses than of hits, CI above 0, the paper may say misses are partly label noise. 17.8% vs 0.9%: +16.9 points (CI +12.1 to +21.4).

explain.asks: When protein search misses the right family, is it really wrong? The family labels (PGfam) are assigned by BV-BRC and can be noisy. Here the top hits are checked by aligning them with the query: is the hit a real homolog?
explain.how: 989 proteins whose family has a gene outside the query's own genus, searched with the genus removed (weighted score, catalogue of 2026-11-20). The top hit and the best same-family gene were each aligned with the query to decide whether they are homologs.
verdict: Pass. The rule, set before the run: if the same-family gene is not detectably homologous in at least 10 points more of the misses than of the hits, with the interval above zero, the misses may be called partly label noise. It is so in 17.8% of misses against 0.9% of hits: +16.9 points (interval +12.1 to +21.4).

By alignment, a homolog comes first for 72.2% of proteins, against 64.2% by family label. Homolog first rises with how close the nearest homolog is: 40% below 40% identity, 51% at 40–60%, 82% at 60–80%, 98% at 80–95%, 100% above.
explain.meaning: The search is better than the family labels make it look: part of its 'misses' are genes whose label doesn't match a real relationship. Its true limit is distant homologs: below about 60% identity, the right relative comes first about half the time or less.
explain.methodNote: This places the gene profile honestly: from 9 numbers per window it finds close and moderately distant homologs (60% identity and up) reliably, and loses the remote ones that alignment tools are built for.

Arms: today's stored profiles; profiles from translation; and from translation with the best of shifts from −30 to +30 aa. A hit is judged a homolog by alignment.

explain.meaning: Neither fix reaches remote homologs. Shifts let unrelated genes find a lucky alignment too, which costs more than it gains. The limit is the low identity itself, not how the windows are built or lined up.

experiments.name: protein-null
experiments.title: p and E for protein hits
experiments.question: How often does a gene of another family score this high against a protein of this length?
experiments.rule: No E if, at 167–332 aa, the median protein's E at its best same-family hit is above 0.01 or the spread between proteins is over 100x. Weighted score: median E 0, spread 27x (unweighted 37x): build.
experiments.note: From 411 real proteins scored against genes of other families, weighted score (rerun 2026-11-20; the null itself rebuilt as version 2). The unweighted run is at commit 9f75afe.

keyNumbers.label: E < 0.01 at best same-family hit, 167–332 aa

explain.asks: A protein search always returns a best hit, related or not. To say how surprising a hit is (its p and E values), the platform needs to know how high genes of unrelated families score. Is that background steady enough to build such values?
explain.how: 411 real proteins with a family label (never stored), compared with the catalogue as the protein search compares them, their own gene left out. For each: its best score against a gene of its own family, and how many genes of other families reach each score. The background for a length band is the mean of those counts.
verdict: A measurement that decided whether to build p and E. The rule, set before the run: no E values if, at 167–332 aa, the median protein's E at its best same-family hit is above 0.01, or the background differs between proteins by more than 100 times. With the weighted score: median E 0 and a spread of 27 times, so p and E were built.
The best same-family hit has E below 0.01 for 64% (50–99 aa), 63%, 64%, 46% (333–499 aa) and 71% (500 aa and over) of proteins.
explain.meaning: For about two proteins in three, the best relative's score is beyond anything unrelated genes reach, so the platform can flag such hits as significant. The rest score within the range of chance and are shown without that confidence.
explain.methodNote: Gives profile-based protein search what alignment tools report as standard: an expectation value for each hit, here estimated from real unrelated genes rather than from theory.

charts.read: Most proteins' best relative scores beyond chance; 333–499 aa proteins least often.

experiments.name: eukaryote-genes
experiments.title: Eukaryote genes from CDS files
experiments.question: Does protein search find eukaryote genes built from their CDS files?
experiments.note: 131 annotated assemblies, 2.25M genes, 209 MB. Yeast 100%. Unweighted score; rerunning needs the CDS files again.

explain.asks: Can the protein search find genes of eukaryotes (fungi, plants, animals), whose genes are split by introns, when their profiles are built from the annotated coding sequences (CDS files) NCBI provides?
explain.how: All 131 annotated eukaryote assemblies in the catalogue (57 fungi, 52 plants, 22 animals; local catalogue of 2026-11-09): 2.25 million genes of 50 aa and up profiled from their CDS files. Then, from 42 assemblies, 10 proteins each were searched for their own gene.
verdict: Pass. No numeric rule was written down. The right gene came first, or tied first, for 96.4% of the 420 proteins (95.2% strictly first); yeast 100%, a plant 98%. By length: 94.4% to 98.9% first or tied.
The weakest assemblies (70% first or tied) were two fish genomes; a search took a median of 8.1 s. The whole gene layer takes 209 MB.
explain.meaning: Eukaryote genes are searchable from their proteins like bacterial ones, at the same accuracy, once their coding sequences are known. Eukaryotes without an annotation (456 of 587 stored) have no gene layer.
explain.methodNote: Introns don't matter to the gene profile once the coding sequence is joined: it reads the gene from its start codon in coding order, which is exactly what a CDS file gives.

experiments.name: gene-match
experiments.title: Reciprocal best genes without a family
experiments.question: Does the gene score alone pair genes with their counterparts in another genome?
experiments.note: Against 0.5% and 0.2% by chance. Weighted score (rerun 2026-11-20): agreement unchanged (unweighted 99.8% and 92.9%, commit f5cb655), 0.5–0.75% fewer reciprocal pairs. Reads the NCBI CDS files, so not runnable from the database.

explain.asks: For genes without a family label, can the gene score alone pair each gene with its counterpart in a related genome, as a reciprocal best hit?
explain.how: Two pairs of related eukaryote genomes from NCBI: two Podospora (fungi) and two Nelumbo (lotus). Each gene's best-scoring gene in the other genome, kept when the choice is mutual (reciprocal best hit). Judged by NCBI's protein names: does the pair share its normalised name? For reference, the same with amino-acid 4-letter word counts, a sequence-based method.
verdict: Pass. The rule, set before the run: at least 70% of the pairs with informative names on both sides must share the name, in both genome pairs. Podospora: 99.7%; Nelumbo: 92.9%; by chance 0.5% and 0.2%.
The amino-acid word counts agree equally often (99.8% and 92.7%) but find somewhat more pairs: 9,291 against 8,879 in Podospora, 18,889 against 17,588 in Nelumbo.
explain.meaning: The gene profile pairs genes with their counterparts reliably, so the platform can match genes between related genomes even where no family label exists. It finds about 5–7% fewer pairs than a protein-word method.
explain.methodNote: Shown beside a sequence-based reference on purpose: the profile matches its accuracy, from far fewer numbers per gene, but not its reach.

charts.help: Among reciprocal best pairs with informative NCBI names on both sides. Two methods: the Z-curve gene score and amino-acid 4-letter word counts.
charts.read: Both methods agree with the names about equally; by chance the share would be under 1%.

experiments.name: search-breakdown
experiments.title: Where a protein search spends its time
experiments.question: Reading, decoding or scoring: what dominates a protein search, and what cut it?
experiments.note: Pooled buffers and scoring in place cut the time above the transfer floor by 58%; PostgreSQL's transfer is now 74–92% of a query.

explain.asks: Where does a protein search spend its time: getting gene profiles out of the database, unpacking them, or scoring them? And what did the changes made to speed it up actually gain?
explain.how: Five protein queries (60 to 700 aa) and five fragment searches on the local catalogue, each stage timed separately (the median of repeated runs), before and after the changes: reading rows into reused buffers and scoring them where they lie (no unpacking), keeping each length band's rows together on disk, and two exact shortcuts that stop scoring early.
verdict: A measurement: no rule. Scoring in place cut the time above the database's transfer floor by 58%; end to end a protein search got 12% faster (2.8 to 7.8 s). The database's transfer is now 74–92% of a query.
Keeping rows together on disk cut reading by 17–18%. The two early-stop shortcuts gained nothing and were removed.
explain.meaning: A protein search is now limited by how fast the database hands over the gene rows, not by the arithmetic: scoring 2 million genes takes about 0.2 s.
explain.methodNote: Shows the method's cost profile: comparing profiles is cheap; moving the stored numbers is the expensive part.

experiments.name: bulk-load
experiments.title: The bulk load
experiments.question: How long does filling the catalogue from BV-BRC take, and how many duplicates are there?
experiments.note: 19,964 stored, 1,982 duplicates skipped (12.6% of viruses), 0 failed; 8.6 h active.
experiments.command: dotnet run --project SequencePlatform.Ingest -- ingest-bvbrc --group bacteria --limit N

explain.asks: How long does filling the catalogue from BV-BRC take, how many genomes turn out to be duplicates, and does anything fail?
explain.how: Every bacterial, archaeal and viral genome on BV-BRC's list for the load (21,946), each downloaded, profiled as it streamed in, stored, and its file deleted, on the laptop over 2026-10-19 and 20.
verdict: A measurement: no rule. 19,964 genomes stored and 1,982 skipped as duplicates of a stored genome, almost all viruses (12.6% of the listed viruses). None failed; 11 bacteria needed one retry. 8.6 hours of active work, 1.46 s per genome, giving 24,365 records (chromosomes, plasmids, segments).
Profiles take 824 MB and the whole database 496 MB on disk, compressed. 10 of 10 random genomes matched BV-BRC on every field checked.
explain.meaning: The catalogue can be rebuilt from scratch in about a working day on a laptop, with no DNA kept.
explain.methodNote: Infrastructure, not the method itself: it shows the no-DNA design works at catalogue scale, since every genome is profiled as it streams in and then discarded.

charts.help: By group of genomes, as listed by BV-BRC for the load.
charts.read: Nearly all duplicates are viruses, many deposited more than once.

terms: Streaming
Reading a sequence piece by piece from the file and keeping only running totals, so the whole sequence never has to fit in memory.

experiments.name: neighbour-ranking
experiments.title: Re-ranking by shared neighbours
experiments.question: Does re-ranking the top 100 by shared top-20 neighbours find more same-genus genomes?
experiments.note: Bacteria p = 0.002; viruses 0.462 → 0.491. Reruns from the database through today's search (SequencePlatform.Experiments/NeighbourRanking.cs), which has added rotation and wrap-around since.

explain.asks: Find-similar ranks genomes by profile score. Would re-ranking its top 100 by shared neighbours put more genomes of the query's genus in the top 10?
explain.how: 150 bacteria and 150 viruses of at least 8 kbp, each with a same-genus genome in its length band, searched through the platform's find-similar with and without re-ranking. Measured: the share of the top 10 from the query's genus (precision at 10) and the rank of the first one.
verdict: Pass, judged by a sign test over queries. For bacteria, re-ranking raises precision at 10 from 0.131 to 0.195, better for 51 queries and worse for 24 (p = 0.002).
For viruses the gain is small and not clear: 0.462 to 0.491, 39 better and 23 worse (p = 0.056).
explain.meaning: Neighbours shared across the catalogue add something a single pairwise score lacks: genomes of the same genus keep the same company. The platform re-ranks every find-similar search this way. Rerun on today's database (below), bacteria still gain (0.229 → 0.293) and viruses don't.
explain.methodNote: Uses the profile's scores twice: once to find each genome's 20 nearest across the catalogue, stored as a graph, and once to rank a query's hits by the neighbours they share.

charts.title: Same-genus genomes in the top 10, by score and re-ranked
charts.help: Mean precision at 10 over 150 queries per kind.
charts.read: Re-ranking lifts bacteria clearly; for viruses the difference is within chance.

terms: Precision at 10
Of the 10 best hits, the share that are right (here: of the same genus as the query).
Reciprocal rank
1 divided by the rank of the first right hit: 1 if it's first, 0.5 if second, and so on.
Sign test
Counts how many cases go one way and how many the other, and asks how unlikely that split would be if each were a coin toss.
Shared neighbours
For every stored genome, the platform keeps its 20 nearest genomes. Re-ranking moves up the candidates whose 20 nearest overlap most with the query's.

experiments.name: rotation-production
experiments.title: Origin rotation in find-similar
experiments.question: Does scoring circular chromosomes from their origin find more same-genus genomes?
experiments.note: Warm E. coli search 76 → 382 ms.

explain.asks: Circular chromosomes are deposited from arbitrary starting points, which costs the score ('Strand and rotation'). Once find-similar also scores each chromosome laid out from its replication origin, does it find more genomes of the same genus?
explain.how: The same 150 bacteria and 150 viruses as the neighbour test, through find-similar before and after origin rotation went live, by score and with neighbour re-ranking.
verdict: Pass. No numeric rule was written down. Bacteria: precision at 10 rises from 0.131 to 0.169 by score, and from 0.195 to 0.231 with neighbour re-ranking (better for 54 queries, worse for 20). Viruses are unchanged: rotation applies to circular chromosomes of 500 kbp and up.
A warm search for E. coli got slower, from 76 to 382 ms, since every candidate is scored in both layouts.
explain.meaning: Laid out from their origin, related bacteria look as related as they are. The cost is a few hundred milliseconds per search.
explain.methodNote: The origin is found from the stored profile itself, by its GC skew ('Replication origin from the profile'), so the fix needs no DNA.

charts.title: Bacteria: same-genus genomes in the top 10, before and after rotation
charts.help: Mean precision at 10 over 150 bacterial queries.
charts.read: Rotation adds to both rankings; the two fixes stack.

Of the 10 best hits, the share that are right (here: of the same genus as the query).

For every stored genome, the platform keeps its 20 nearest genomes. Re-ranking moves up the candidates whose 20 nearest overlap most with the query's.

experiments.name: wrap-around
experiments.title: Circularly permuted viruses
experiments.question: Does scoring a virus candidate wrapped around its end find more same-genus viruses?
experiments.note: 1.15× the time. Skipping neighbour re-ranking for viruses was checked and not taken. The AUC check reruns from the database (SequencePlatform.Experiments/CircularPermutation.cs); precision@10 is from the search script.

keyNumbers.label: AUC same genus vs other family, before

explain.asks: Many phage genomes are circularly permuted. Would scoring each virus candidate as if wrapped around its end (its windows followed by themselves again) find more viruses of the same genus?
explain.how: 400 viruses with a same-genus genome in their length band (10,559 in the pool, local catalogue of 2026-11-12), scored against every candidate plainly and wrapped. Then 300 searches through find-similar, and a check of neighbour re-ranking for viruses.
verdict: Pass. The rule, set before the run: stop if the AUC gains less than 0.005 and the top 10 changes by less than 2%. AUC (same genus against other families) rose from 0.904 to 0.934, better for 167 queries and worse for 49; same-genus genomes in the top 10 from 6.3 to 7.1; 40% of top-10 hits changed. Through find-similar, precision at 10 went from 0.597 to 0.670, at 1.15 times the time.

The gain goes to related pairs: 22.8% of same-genus pairs rise by more than 0.03, against 1.2% of pairs from other families. Neighbour re-ranking was checked for viruses too: it slightly lowers the first right hit (reciprocal rank 0.867 by score, 0.827 re-ranked) and was left in place.
explain.meaning: For viruses, where circular permutation is common, wrapping lets related genomes line up, and almost only related ones gain.
explain.methodNote: A fix that comes from the profile's structure: windows are kept in order, so wrapping is just repeating them. Unrelated genomes have nothing to line up and barely move.

charts.title: 400 viruses: plain and wrapped scoring
charts.help: AUC for same genus against other families, and the reciprocal rank of the first same-genus hit, averaged over queries.

measure.mean_auc_genus_vs_other_family: AUC, same genus vs other families
measure.mean_reciprocal_rank_first_same_genus: Reciprocal rank of the first same-genus hit

charts.read: Both measures rise with wrapping. Counts of queries that got better and worse are in the table.
