charts.help: 300 virus searches, by score alone and with neighbour re-ranking (the platform's default).
charts.read: Wrapping raises both rankings by about 0.07 to 0.10.

terms: AUC

A score for how well a ranking puts the right items first: 0.5 is a coin toss, 1 is perfect. Here it is the chance that a randomly picked related pair scores closer than a randomly picked unrelated pair.
Precision at 10
Of the 10 best hits, the share that are right (here: of the same genus as the query).
Reciprocal rank
1 divided by the rank of the first right hit: 1 if it's first, 0.5 if second, and so on.
Circular permutation
The same circular genome deposited starting at different points, so one copy's start is in the middle of another's. Common among phages.

experiments.name: second-order
experiments.title: The second-order Z-curve equals Karlin ρ*
experiments.question: Do Z-curve means and lag-1 covariances rebuild the dinucleotide signature exactly?
experiments.note: log ρ* in Z-curve axes is a rotation: same trees, map |r| = 1.000000. Dropping the 7 neighbour coefficients is what made the incomplete form trail.

explain.asks: Karlin's dinucleotide signature can be rewritten in Z-curve form: the Z-curve averages plus how each axis relates to the next base's. Is that an exact rewrite, and do shortened forms lose anything?
explain.how: Several ways of writing a genome's dinucleotide signature, from Karlin's original to Z-curve forms keeping all or only some of the coefficients, compared on 5,480 catalogue genomes (how often a genome's nearest neighbour shares its genus, family or phylum) and on the bundled genomes (AUC, and which clades trees recover).
verdict: Pass. No numeric rule was written down. With all 16 coefficients the Z-curve form is exactly Karlin's signature, turned in space: the same trees and the same map (|r| = 1.000000).

Shortened forms trail it: nearest neighbour in the same genus 30.1–30.6% against 31.6%, in the same family 45.1–45.8% against 47.5%. What they drop is information from neighbouring bases, not composition.
explain.meaning: The Z-curve is a coordinate system that contains the classic dinucleotide signature exactly; it doesn't add to it. The platform stores the signature this way and can show it in Z-curve or Karlin view, which are the same map turned.
explain.methodNote: Not a gain for the Z-curve method, and stated as such: the Z-curve gives a different view of Karlin's signature here, not a better one.

charts.title: Nearest neighbour of the same taxon, by form of the signature
charts.help: 5,480 bacteria and archaea of the catalogue: the share whose nearest genome by each form shares their genus, family or phylum.
charts.read: Karlin and the full Z-curve form are identical; the shortened forms are a point or two lower.

terms: log ρ* (dinucleotide signature)
Karlin's genomic signature: for each of the 16 two-base words (AA, AC, …), how much more or less often it occurs than the genome's base composition predicts. Close relatives have similar signatures.
Z-curve

A way of writing DNA as a path in three dimensions, one axis for each pair of base properties: purine (A, G) against pyrimidine (C, T), amino (A, C) against keto (G, T), and strong (G, C) against weak (A, T) pairing. The third axis is GC content.

experiments.name: relatives
experiments.title: Nearest relatives
experiments.question: Are a genome's 10 nearest signatures its relatives?
experiments.note: 4–9 ms per query.

keyNumbers.label: E. coli K-12: Escherichia/Shigella in its 10

explain.asks: Are a genome's 10 nearest by signature, the platform's 'relatives' view, its real relatives? And is the answer fast enough to show as you browse?
explain.how: An index of 19,935 genomes (6,375 bacteria and archaea, 13,560 viruses; one record per genome, plasmids left out) by dinucleotide signature. Checks on E. coli K-12 and SARS-CoV-2, query times, and the time to draw trees of 500 genomes.
verdict: Pass, against limits set beforehand for speed (100 ms a query, 5 s a tree) and at least 1 relative in 10. E. coli K-12's 10 nearest include 9 Escherichia or Shigella; SARS-CoV-2's 10 are all coronaviruses.

A query takes a median of 3.9 ms (bacteria) and 9.0 ms (viruses). A 500-genome tree takes 0.4 s by UPGMA and 1.0 s by neighbour joining, once its distance matrix was kept as an array (7 to 12 s before, over the limit).
explain.meaning: The signature's nearest neighbours are sensible relatives and come back instantly, so the platform shows relatives and trees live. Since 2026-11-22, bacteria, archaea and viruses with a gene layer use amino-acid CVTree vectors instead, which put 13 to 16 more points of the same genus among the 10 nearest.
explain.methodNote: This feature uses whole-genome signatures (log ρ*, and now CVTree), not the windowed Z-curve profile: one vector per genome is what makes an instant index of 20,000 genomes possible.
terms: log ρ* (dinucleotide signature)
Karlin's genomic signature: for each of the 16 two-base words (AA, AC, …), how much more or less often it occurs than the genome's base composition predicts. Close relatives have similar signatures.

experiments.name: e2-phage-host
experiments.title: Phage host from the signature
experiments.question: Does the dinucleotide signature or localization tell a phage's host genus?
experiments.note: Passes its rule, fixed before the run: beats GC with the 95% lower bound above 0, overall (+0.033) and macro (+0.031). A weak pass: always guessing Escherichia gives 0.110, which the rule didn't test. Localization: 0/200. Round 2 (e2b, 6-mers) passes. Predictor A reruns from the database (SequencePlatform.Experiments/PhageHost.cs); localization stays in the script.

explain.asks: A phage's DNA composition tends to drift towards its host's. Can the platform guess a phage's host genus from composition alone, as the stored genus whose genome is nearest to the phage?
how: 4,419 phages whose recorded host genus is among the genera stored in the catalogue. For each phage, every stored genus is ranked by the distance from the phage to that genus's nearest genome, by signature. A hit is the recorded host genus ranked first.

Three baselines: GC alone, always guessing the commonest host genus (Escherichia), and the signature with host labels shuffled between phages. 'Averaged over host genera' gives each of the 69 host genera with at least 5 phages the same weight, so the many Escherichia phages don't dominate.
verdict: Pass, but a weak one. The rule, set before the run: the signature must beat GC, with the 95% interval of the difference above zero, both over all phages and averaged over host genera. It does: 5.7% against 2.4% (+3.3 points, interval +2.5 to +4.1), and averaged over genera 4.4% against 1.3% (+3.1, interval +1.8 to +4.4).

The rule didn't include the commonest-host guess, and over all phages that guess does better: always saying Escherichia is right 11.0% of the time. Averaged over host genera, where that trick stops working (1.5%), the signature leads.
A second approach, finding the phage's own DNA inside a stored host genome (a prophage), gave no confident hit for any of 200 sampled phages.
explain.meaning: Dinucleotide composition carries a weak host signal: about 2.5 times GC's hit rate, but well below a simple guess over all phages, so it isn't usable as a host predictor on its own. Longer words do better: in a follow-up test, 6-letter words get the host genus first for 21% of phages and beat the commonest-host guess.
explain.methodNote: This tests log ρ*, Karlin's dinucleotide signature, which the platform stores for every genome, not the windowed Z-curve profile. The prophage search did use the Z-curve profile, and found nothing that this test could count.

charts.title: Host genus ranked first
charts.help: The share of phages whose recorded host genus is the first guess, over all phages and averaged over the 69 host genera with at least 5 phages.
charts.read: Over all phages, always guessing Escherichia beats the signature, because so many stored phages infect Escherichia. Averaged over host genera, that guess falls to 1.5% and the signature leads. Shuffled labels show what chance alone gives.

terms: log ρ* (dinucleotide signature)
Karlin's genomic signature: for each of the 16 two-base words (AA, AC, …), how much more or less often it occurs than the genome's base composition predicts. Close relatives have similar signatures.
Top 1
The right answer is ranked first.
95% interval
The range the true value most likely lies in, estimated by resampling the data many times (bootstrap). A difference whose interval doesn't include zero is unlikely to be chance.
Shuffle
The same calculation with the labels randomly reassigned, repeated many times: it shows what chance alone gives.

experiments.name: e3-islands
experiments.title: Genomic islands
experiments.question: Do windows that deviate from their genome mark genomic islands better than GC?

explain.asks: Can the profile's windows mark genomic islands better than GC content alone?
how: Every 500 bp window of 2,176 chromosomes (20 million windows) scored by how far its local composition, averaged over 4 kbp, sits from the genome's own, using all three Z-curve axes, or GC alone. Answer key: islands found by IslandPick, which compares related genomes and so doesn't use composition; a curated set of 18 genomes as a second key.
Genomes were split in half: each detector's cut-off chosen on one half and tested on the other.
verdict: Fail. The rule, set before the run: the Z-curve detector's F1 on the test half must beat GC's, with the 95% interval of the difference above zero. It is lower: 0.128 against 0.153 (difference −0.025, interval −0.028 to −0.023). Measured against the genome's mean instead of a running baseline, GC still leads (0.207 against 0.161).
The two non-GC axes alone do worst (0.085).
explain.meaning: For spotting foreign DNA by composition, GC alone is the better signal, and the other two axes add noise. Every composition detector is weak here (F1 0.09 to 0.21, against 4.4% of windows being island), since many islands look like their host.
explain.methodNote: A plain negative for the windowed profile on the question it seemed made for: an unusual window is better caught by GC alone.

charts.title: Island windows found (F1, test half), by detector
charts.help: Against IslandPick's islands on 1,088 test genomes. 'Running baseline' compares each window with the surrounding 100 kbp; 'genome mean' with the whole genome.
charts.read: GC alone is ahead with either baseline; the curated 18-genome key, in the table, tells the same story.

terms: GC content
The share of G and C among a genome's bases. It ranges from about 25% to 75% across bacteria and is the simplest measure of composition.
95% interval
The range the true value most likely lies in, estimated by resampling the data many times (bootstrap). A difference whose interval doesn't include zero is unlikely to be chance.
Genomic island
A stretch of a bacterial genome gained from another organism, often carrying genes for resistance, virulence or new metabolism. Islands often differ in composition from their host.
F1
One number combining precision (how many flagged windows really are islands) and recall (how many island windows were flagged); 1 is perfect.

experiments.name: e5-habitat
experiments.title: Habitat beyond genus and GC
experiments.question: Do signature neighbours share a habitat more than a within-genus shuffle predicts?
experiments.note: 82 of 108 genera above the shuffle, p = 3·10⁻⁸. Reruns from the database (SequencePlatform.Experiments/Habitat.cs). E5b's richer signatures (6-mers, amino-acid composition, CVTree) don't beat log ρ*.

keyNumbers.label: genera where the signature beats GC

explain.asks: Related genomes look alike, so any composition signature groups bacteria by ancestry. But do genomes from the same kind of place look alike beyond that? Within one genus, where ancestry is roughly shared, are a genome's closest neighbours by signature more often from its own habitat (soil, marine, clinical and so on) than chance predicts?
how: 3,744 bacterial and archaeal genomes in 108 genera. Each genus has at least 10 genomes whose isolation source names a habitat (clinical, food, host-associated, marine, freshwater, soil), and at least two habitats.

For each genome, its 5 nearest genomes of the same genus by signature; the score is the share of them from its own habitat. Chance is measured by shuffling the habitat labels within the genus 1,000 times, which keeps the genus's ancestry but breaks any link to habitat.
verdict: Pass. The rule, set before the run: more genera above the shuffle than below, by a one-sided sign test at p < 0.05. 82 of 108 genera are above and 26 below (p = 3 × 10⁻⁸).

Beside the rule: on average 51% of a genome's nearest neighbours share its habitat, against 47% when the labels are shuffled. GC alone, used the same way, also beats the shuffle, but less (excess 0.035 against 0.047).
meaning: Within a genus, genomes from the same kind of place share a little more composition than chance: habitat leaves a mark on the signature. The effect is small, a few points per genus, so it shows a tendency across many genomes, not a way to tell one genome's habitat.

Part of it may still be ancestry below the genus: species within a genus often live in different places. Richer signatures (6-letter words, amino-acid composition, CVTree) were tried later on the same genera, and none does clearly better.
explain.methodNote: This tests log ρ*, Karlin's dinucleotide signature, which the platform stores for every genome, not the windowed Z-curve profile. The platform holds it in Z-curve coordinates, but those are the same numbers turned in space, so nothing here is a gain of the Z-curve method. It shows what the stored signature says about biology.

charts.title: Each genus: same-habitat neighbours, observed against chance
charts.help: One dot per genus. Up: how often a genome's 5 nearest neighbours in its genus share its habitat. Across: the same with habitat labels shuffled within the genus.
charts.name: Taxon
charts.read: On the dashed diagonal, neighbours share a habitat exactly as often as chance. Above it, more often. Most genera sit a little above the line, not far above it: the effect is consistent but small.

terms: log ρ* (dinucleotide signature)
Karlin's genomic signature: for each of the 16 two-base words (AA, AC, …), how much more or less often it occurs than the genome's base composition predicts. Close relatives have similar signatures.
Shuffle
The same calculation with the labels randomly reassigned, repeated many times: it shows what chance alone gives.
Sign test
Counts how many genera go one way and how many the other, and asks how unlikely that split would be if each were a coin toss.

experiments.name: insert-check
experiments.title: Inserts between two genomes
experiments.question: Can two genomes' profiles show what one has that the other lacks?
experiments.note: Rule: ≥ 80% of inserts ≥ 10 kbp at ≤ 1 false call per Mbp. Same-GC donors are missed.

explain.asks: Given two related genomes' profiles, can the platform show what one has that the other lacks: inserted stretches of foreign DNA?
explain.how: E. coli K-12's profile against copies of K-12 carrying 16 inserts each (2, 5, 10 and 20 kbp) from four unrelated donors of different GC (Vibrio, B. subtilis, P. aeruginosa, S. aureus); 10 copies. A comparative detector places every 4 kbp block of the copy in K-12 and flags blocks that don't fit; a GC detector flags windows of unusual GC. Cut-offs come from a copy with no inserts.
explain.verdict: Fail. The rule, set before the run: find at least 80% of inserts of 10 kbp and up, with at most 1 false call per Mbp. The comparative detector found 72.5% (85% of 20 kbp inserts, 60% of 10 kbp ones) with 2.27 false calls per Mbp. It finds inserts from donors of very different GC (S. aureus and P. aeruginosa: all from 10 kbp) and misses those of similar GC (Vibrio: none at 10 kbp, 40% at 20 kbp). GC alone found 11%.
explain.meaning: Comparing two profiles shows inserts only when the donor's composition differs from the host's; inserts that look like the host stay invisible. It isn't a reliable way to find gained DNA.
explain.methodNote: Far better than GC alone (72.5% against 11%), because it uses the order of windows, but still limited by composition: a profile can't tell apart two different stretches of the same local makeup.

charts.title: Inserts found by comparing profiles, by donor
charts.help: 10 inserts per donor and length. E. coli K-12, the host, is 50.8% GC.
charts.read: The further the donor's GC from the host's, the more inserts are found; Vibrio, closest to E. coli, is almost invisible.

terms: GC content
The share of G and C among a genome's bases. It ranges from about 25% to 75% across bacteria and is the simplest measure of composition.

experiments.name: kmer-check
experiments.title: Longer k-mers for phage hosts
experiments.question: Do 3- to 6-mers tell a phage's host better than dinucleotides?
experiments.note: 207 phages and hosts streamed from NCBI and counted without keeping DNA. Led to storing 6-mer counts.

explain.asks: Phage host prediction from dinucleotides was weak. Would longer words (3 to 6 letters) tell a phage's host better, enough to justify downloading the catalogue again to count them?
explain.how: A sample: for each host genus with at least 5 phages, 3 phages and 3 host genomes (207 of each, 69 genera), streamed from NCBI and counted as they arrived, keeping no DNA. Each phage's host is guessed as the genus of its nearest host genome, by word frequencies, or by how far words deviate from what shorter words predict (k = 2 to 6).
explain.verdict: Pass. The rule, set before the run: a re-download is worth it only if the best word length beats dinucleotides (log ρ*) by at least 5 points of top-1 with the 95% interval above zero. 6-letter word frequencies reach 25.6% against 15.0% (+10.6 points, interval +5.3 to +15.9). GC alone: 5.8%.
explain.meaning: Longer words carry more of the host's signal. This led the platform to store 6-letter word counts for every genome; the full test on 7,461 phages confirmed it (6-letter words 21.2% against 5.7% for dinucleotides).
explain.methodNote: Tests classic word-count signatures, not the Z-curve profile, and keeps the platform's no-DNA rule: sequences were counted as they streamed in and never stored.

charts.title: Host genus ranked first, by signature
charts.help: 207 phages, 69 host genera. 'Markov' signatures measure how far each word deviates from what shorter words predict (k = 2 is log ρ*); 'frequency' uses the word frequencies themselves.
charts.read: Frequencies keep improving up to 6 letters; Markov deviations peak at 3. GC alone is far behind.

terms: log ρ* (dinucleotide signature)
Karlin's genomic signature: for each of the 16 two-base words (AA, AC, …), how much more or less often it occurs than the genome's base composition predicts. Close relatives have similar signatures.
95% interval
The range the true value most likely lies in, estimated by resampling the data many times (bootstrap). A difference whose interval doesn't include zero is unlikely to be chance.
k-mer (word) counts
How often each word of k letters (AAAAAA, AAAAAC, …) occurs in a genome. Longer words carry more detail; 6-letter words have 2,080 forms when a word and its reverse complement count together.
